body:
OBJECTIVES
- Students use maps to explain how the locations of oases, mountains and deserts shaped the routes of the Silk Roads (D2.Geo.2.6-8).
- Students explain how changes in transportation and trade connected distant places (D2.Geo.7.6-8).
- Students explain multiple effects of the spread of beliefs and technologies along the routes (D2.His.14.6-8), developing the topic with well-chosen facts and examples (WHST.6-8.2.B).
- Students explain how paper money made exchange easier (D2.Eco.5.6-8).
- Students identify an author's point of view and purpose and detect limits in a traveler's account (RH.6-8.6, D2.His.10.6-8).

MATERIALS
- Routes of the Silk Roads (lesson reading)
- Marco Polo on Paper Money (assessment source)
- A blank outline map of Afro-Eurasia, colored pencils
- Cards for a relay-trade simulation (each card is a good; each table is a market town)
- A cause-and-effect organizer: idea, how it traveled, effect

FIVE-DAY PLAN
Day 1: Read the overview. Relay-trade simulation: a "bolt of silk" passes through five tables, and each table adds to its price. Debrief: why did prices rise, and why did so few people travel the whole route? Begin the lesson, Mapping the Silk Roads.
Day 2: Finish the lesson maps. Mini-lecture with images: Buddhism moving from India into China, paper-making moving west, and later the plague moving along the same routes.
Day 3: Students plan Ideas on the Move with the cause-and-effect organizer and draft their first example.
Day 4: Finish and revise Ideas on the Move. Peer check: does each example name the idea, how it traveled, and its effect?
Day 5: Assessment: Paper Money in the Great Khan's China. Remind students that sourcing counts as much as content.

DIFFERENTIATION
- Support: give a map with the main cities already labeled, and a word bank (Chang'an, Dunhuang, Kashgar, Samarkand, Merv). Offer a paragraph frame for each example: "___ spread from ___ to ___ when ___. As a result, ___."
- Support: read the Marco Polo source aloud and chunk it into three parts with a gist sentence for each.
- Stretch: research the maritime Silk Road through the Indian Ocean and compare its advantages with the land routes.
- Multilingual learners: label map routes with arrows and pictures of goods; pre-teach caravan, oasis and currency with images; allow students to discuss the sourcing questions in their home language before writing in English.

FAMILY NOTE (send home at the start of the unit)
We are studying the Silk Roads, the trade routes that linked China and the Mediterranean for more than a thousand years. Your child will learn that traders carried not only silk and spices but also religions, inventions and even diseases. Ask your child to look around your kitchen or home for one food, invention or idea that first came from far away, and to tell you how it might have traveled.
title: Teacher guide: The Silk Roads
